notation: Labbe's Q (process variance) is R_proc in this package; Labbe's R (measurement variance) is Q_meas. Every note that quotes the book's Q or R says which one it is.

items.anchor: One Dimensional Kalman Filters
items.note: Skim the intro, 3 min. Read the notation table in map.md first: Labbe's Q is our R_proc, Labbe's R is our Q_meas, the opposite of Thrun's letters. No equations in this chapter are numbered, so the package cites page and section.

items.anchor: a Bayesian filter that uses Gaussians
items.note: WHY: this is the whole chapter in six words. Predict and update from the discrete Bayes filter (t2.1) stay; the belief becomes two numbers (mean, variance) instead of a histogram. LINK: Thrun Table 3.1 (gold package t2.2) is the same loop with matrices.

items.anchor: Problem Description
items.note: Skim. The dog in a hallway with an RFID position sensor: a 1-D state measured directly, so the measurement function is the identity. Keep that in mind; it is why the likelihood on p. 137 is a Gaussian centred on z.

items.anchor: the errors seemed to be evenly distributed on both sides of the true position
items.note: DEFINE: this is the zero-mean (unbiased) noise assumption, stated informally. ROBOT: a wheel encoder on a slipping track or a baro altimeter with a temperature drift has biased error; the Gaussian model here cannot absorb a bias, it needs a bias state (Labbe ch. 6 onward).

items.anchor: We predict that the dog is moving. This prediction is not perfect.
items.note: DEFINE: the process model has its own error, also modelled as Gaussian. Its variance becomes R_proc (Labbe's Q) on p. 145. Two noise sources, two variances: everything the chapter does is a trade between them.

items.anchor: Beliefs as Gaussians
items.note: Skip; covered in Labbe ch. 3. N(10, 1) and 500 random draws, nothing new for this package.

items.anchor: Tracking with Gaussian Probabilities
items.note: Must read, 10 min. Take the table on p. 134: predict becomes a sum of Gaussians, update becomes a product. The rest of the chapter checks that both stay Gaussian.

items.anchor: Tracking was performed with a cycle of predictions and updates
items.note: LINK: t2.1, the discrete Bayes filter (Labbe ch. 2). Predict = convolution with the motion kernel, update = likelihood times prior, normalise. Both steps survive unchanged; only the representation of the belief changes.

items.anchor: led to histograms that implied the dog could be in multiple places at once
items.note: PITFALL: the book calls multimodality a defect. On a robot it is often the truth: global localisation on the RoboCup field (symmetric halves), a kidnapped robot, an ambiguous lidar match. A single Gaussian cannot say "one of two places"; that is what particle filters (Thrun ch. 4) and multi-hypothesis trackers are for.

items.anchor: We can replace hundreds to thousands of numbers with a single pair of numbers
items.note: WHY: the cost argument. The histogram predict is a convolution over all bins per step; the Gaussian predict is two additions. COST: O(1) per step in 1-D. In n-D this becomes O(n^3) for the covariance, still independent of the size of the world.

items.anchor: In this chapter we replace histograms with Gaussians
items.note: DERIVE: the table below this sentence is the plan of the chapter. Predict: x̄ = x ⊕ f_x (sum, p. 135). Update: x = L ⊗ x̄ (product, p. 137). CODE: card C1 (predict) and card C2 (update, Bayes form).

items.anchor: This will only work if the sum and product of two Gaussians is another Gaussian
items.note: WHY: closure is the reason the Kalman filter has a closed form. It holds for linear motion and linear measurement with Gaussian noise; the EKF and UKF (Labbe ch. 10–11) exist because a nonlinear robot model breaks it.

items.anchor: Predictions with Gaussians
items.note: Must read, 10 min. Take: μ̄ = μ + μ_fx, σ̄² = σ² + σ²_fx. Predict always widens the belief.

items.anchor: the epoch is 2 seconds long
items.note: PITFALL (book): the epoch changes between paragraphs. Here Δt = 2 s gives x̄ = 40; four lines down Δt = 1 s gives f_x = N(15, 0.7²) and x̄ = 25 (p. 136). The worked numbers on p. 136–137 use the 1 s epoch.

items.anchor: μ = μ1 + μ2
items.note: DERIVE: the sum of two independent Gaussian random variables: means add, variances add. This is a sum of random variables (convolution of the pdfs), not a sum of pdfs; adding two pdfs gives a two-bump mixture. Independence of x and f_x is assumed. CODE: card C1, `predict`.

items.anchor: We don't really know where the dog is moving, so the confidence should get smaller
items.note: WHY: predict never shrinks the variance, update never grows it. Any filter of yours where P falls during predict has a bug. TEST: a natural invariant test: P̄ ≥ P after every predict, P ≤ P̄ after every update.

items.anchor: is the amount of uncertainty added to the system due to the imperfect prediction
items.note: DEFINE: σ²_fx, the variance added per predict. This is R_proc (Labbe's Q, p. 151). ROBOT: for wheel odometry it grows with distance travelled and with slip; on the tracked robot it is much larger in a turn than on a straight.

items.anchor: def predict(pos, movement):
items.note: CODE: card C1, `predict(x, P, u, R_proc)`. Two additions. The book's `movement` is a Gaussian (u, R_proc); the package passes them as two numbers, as FilterPy does (p. 168).

items.anchor: The prior states that the dog is at 25 m with a variance of 0.53
items.note: TEST: oracle from the book cell, p. 137: predict(N(10, 0.2²), N(15, 0.7²)) = N(25, 0.53). 0.04 + 0.49 = 0.53, so it also checks that you added variances, not standard deviations (0.2 + 0.7 = 0.9 is the classic bug).

items.anchor: Updates with Gaussians
items.note: Must read, 15 min. Take the posterior mean and variance on p. 138 and the fact that the variance does not depend on z.

items.anchor: The likelihood is the probability of the measurement given the current state
items.note: DEFINE: p(z | x), read as a function of x for the z you got. It is N(z, σ_z²) in x only because the sensor measures x directly (h(x) = x). PITFALL: with a range-bearing sensor the likelihood in x is not a Gaussian centred on z; that is the EKF's job (Labbe ch. 11).

items.anchor: the product of two Gaussians is proportional to another Gausian
items.note: WHY: "proportional" hides a constant, N(z; μ̄, σ̄² + σ_z²): the probability of the measurement before you saw it. The chapter drops it; robots use it for outlier gating and NIS (lecture, exercises). The spelling "Gausian" is the book's.

items.anchor: We put this in Bayesian terms like so
items.note: DERIVE: the Bayes-form update. μ = (σ̄²μ_z + σ_z²μ̄)/(σ̄² + σ_z²), σ² = σ̄²σ_z²/(σ̄² + σ_z²). Each mean is weighted by the other's variance. CODE: card C2, `update_bayes`. Derive by hand that it equals the gain form on p. 149.

items.anchor: def gaussian_multiply(g1, g2):
items.note: CODE: card C2. Symmetric in g1 and g2: the filter cannot tell a measurement from a prior, which is the point of p. 141. TEST: swapping the arguments gives the same result.

items.anchor: the variances are completely unaffected by the values of the mean
items.note: WHY: the variance sequence P̄₁, P₁, P̄₂, ... does not depend on the data. You can compute it offline; that is why it converges (p. 146, 148) and why the fixed-gain filter on p. 167 works. PITFALL: true only for linear models; in an EKF the Jacobians depend on the estimate, so P does too.

items.anchor: estimated_pos = update(predicted_pos, measured_pos)
items.note: TEST: oracle from the book cell, p. 138: update(N(10, 0.2²), N(11, 0.1²)) = N(10.8, 0.008). The measurement is four times more precise in variance, so it takes 4/5 of the weight.

items.anchor: Understanding Gaussian Multiplication
items.note: Skim, 10 min with p. 140–142. Two facts: the product is narrower than both inputs, and it sits nearer the narrower one. The session lets you drag both.

items.anchor: I am more confident with two measurements than with one
items.note: TEST: book oracle, p. 139: N(10, 1) × N(10, 1) = N(10, 0.5). In information form 1/σ² = 1/1 + 1/1 = 2: information adds, which is the cleanest way to remember the update variance.

items.anchor: ({g2.mean},{ge.var})
items.note: PITFALL (book): typo in the legend string; it is not an f-string and says `ge.var`, so every plot from `plot_products` prints the literal text instead of the second Gaussian's parameters (p. 140–142). Read the parameters from the code cell.

items.anchor: It doesn't matter if we are incorporating information from two measurements, or a measurement and a prediction, the math is the same
items.note: WHY: the update is sensor fusion. A prior is just another measurement of x. ROBOT: fusing two altimeters on the drone and fusing a baro reading into a prediction are the same function call.

items.anchor: Perhaps a more reasonable assumption would be that one person made a mistake
items.note: PITFALL: a Gaussian update cannot reject a gross error; it averages it in. ROBOT: a lidar return off glass or a GPS multipath jump pulls the estimate. The fix is a gate on the normalised innovation (NIS), not covered in this chapter; the exercises add it.

items.anchor: notice how the result is far closer to the the input with the smaller variance
items.note: WHY: weights are inverse variances. This sentence is the Kalman gain before it has a name (p. 150). "the the" is the book's.

items.anchor: Interactive Example
items.note: Skim. The ipywidgets cell does not run in the PDF; the package session has the same sliders for two Gaussians and their product.

items.anchor: First Kalman Filter
items.note: Must read, 25 min with the Code Walkthrough. Run the loop on p. 143 by hand for the first row of the table on p. 144.

items.anchor: process_var = 1. # variance in the dog's movement
items.note: DEFINE: Labbe's process variance (his Q) = R_proc in the package. Added every predict, whether or not the dog moved.

items.anchor: sensor_var = 2. # variance in the sensor
items.note: DEFINE: Labbe's sensor variance (his R) = Q_meas in the package. A variance, in m², not a standard deviation.

items.anchor: process_model = gaussian(velocity*dt, process_var)
items.note: PITFALL: the mean scales with dt, the variance does not. With dt = 1 nobody notices. ROBOT: on a robot whose loop runs at a jittery rate, R_proc must scale with dt (white-noise velocity gives variance ∝ dt); Labbe ch. 7 derives it.

items.anchor: prior = predict(x, process_model)
items.note: DERIVE: the whole filter is this three-line loop: predict, build the likelihood from z, update. CODE: card C3 runs it. TEST: the variance column on p. 144 is data-independent (p. 138), so it is a clean oracle to three decimals.

TEST: first row of the book's table. P̄ = 400 + 1 = 401; then P = 401·2/403 = 1.990 and the mean lands at 1.352, almost on z = 1.354, because K = 401/403 ≈ 0.995. Do this row by hand before reading p. 146.

items.anchor: final estimate: 15.053
items.note: TEST: the variance column reaches 1.000 / 2.000 (posterior / prior) by row 8 and stays there for any measurements. The map's fixed-point run gives P∞ = 1.00000 for R_proc = 1, Q_meas = 2.

items.anchor: The filter then forms an estimate part way between the two
items.note: WHY: K ∈ (0, 1), so the posterior mean is always between prior and measurement. TEST: assert min(x̄, z) ≤ x ≤ max(x̄, z) on every step.

items.anchor: Code Walkthrough
items.note: Must read (part of First Kalman Filter). Take what each variance means physically and the first-step numbers on p. 146.

items.anchor: These are not 'magic' numbers; the square root of the variance is the distance error in meters
items.note: WHY: a variance is a physical claim in units². R_proc = 1 m² says "the dog strays about 1 m per step". ROBOT: tune by asking what the std means in metres per step or volts per sample, not by sweeping numbers.

items.anchor: If this was a robot responding to digital commands the performance would be much better
items.note: PITFALL: a commanded velocity is not an achieved one. On the tracked robot, track slip in a turn makes the commanded displacement wrong by tens of percent; R_proc from a datasheet servo spec is optimistic. Measure it.

items.anchor: I believe with 99.7% accuracy the position is 0 plus or minus 60 meters
items.note: WHY: P0 is a statement of how wrong x0 may be. σ = 20 m, ±3σ covers 99.7%. A huge P0 is the honest way to say "no idea": the first update then trusts z almost fully (p. 146).

items.anchor: If this is a robot then this would be a control input to the robot
items.note: LINK: the movement mean is the control term u, Thrun's B·u_t (Table 3.1, gold package). ROBOT: wheel-odometry displacement or an integrated IMU increment.

items.anchor: The variance got worse, which is what always happens during the prediction step
items.note: WHY: 400 → 401. Predict adds R_proc; nothing in it can reduce uncertainty. Same rule as the discrete Bayes predict, which blurred the histogram.

items.anchor: so the filter estimates the position to be very close to the measurement: 1.352
items.note: WHY: P̄ = 401 vs Q_meas = 2 puts K ≈ 0.995 on the first step. A large P0 makes the filter initialise itself from z₁; that is the mechanism behind p. 162–163.

items.anchor: The variance has converged to 1.0
items.note: DERIVE: the fixed point of predict+update, P² + R_proc·P − R_proc·Q_meas = 0, gives P∞ = 1 for R_proc = 1, Q_meas = 2 (map.md run: 1.00000). The book observes the convergence; the lecture derives it. CODE: card C4.

items.anchor: Now look at the plot. The noisy measurements are plotted with black circles
items.note: FIGURE: black circles = z, blue line = posterior mean, red triangles = prior mean. Check each step: blue lies between its triangle and its circle. The lecture redraws it with the package colours (blue estimate, coral measurement).

items.anchor: pos  = (var*z + sensor_var*pos) / (var + sensor_var)
items.note: DERIVE: the five-line filter in Bayes form. Note `var` is the prior variance here because the predict line just overwrote it. CODE: card C2 robust version names both P̄ and P so the two are never confused.

items.anchor: book_plots.plot_filter(xs[:, 0], var=priors[:, 1])
items.note: PITFALL: the shaded band uses the prior variance (priors[:, 1]), while the printed numbers on p. 148 are posterior variances (xs). The band converges to P̄∞ = P∞ + R_proc ≈ 4.16, not 2.16. Label which one you plot.

items.anchor: for a real Kalman filter of course you will not be randomly changing these values
items.note: WHY: R_proc = 2, Q_meas = 4.5 for this run. These are the numbers behind the 2.1623 on p. 148.

items.anchor: Here we can see that the variance converges to 2.1623 in 9 steps
items.note: TEST: book output, p. 148; the map's fixed-point run gives 2.16228 for R_proc = 2, Q_meas = 4.5. The number does not depend on the seed or the data (p. 138).

items.anchor: the filter quickly converges to an estimate with lower variance than the sensor
items.note: WHY: the prediction carries information from all past measurements, so the posterior beats any single reading. That is the only reason to filter at all.

items.anchor: Exercise: Modify Variance Values
items.note: EXERCISE: in the package (exercises, steady-state tier). Write down your guess for which pair gives the smaller variance before running anything; the package computes both fixed points from the steady-state equation (p. 146 note).

items.anchor: KF Animation
items.note: Skip; the animation does not render in the PDF (p. 149 shows a missing image). The session animates the same filter.

items.anchor: Kalman Gain
items.note: Must read, 20 min. Take K = σ̄²/(σ̄² + σ_z²), the residual form μ̄ + K(z − μ̄), and the three variance forms on p. 150.

items.anchor: The weights sum to one because the denominator is a normalization term
items.note: WHY: W1 + W2 = 1 makes the update a convex combination: the posterior is always between prior and measurement (p. 145). It also means one number, K, says everything.

items.anchor: μ = Kμz + (1 −K)¯μ
items.note: DERIVE: from the Bayes form on p. 138 to the gain form, by splitting the fraction into W1 μ_z + W2 μ̄. Do it by hand; it is three lines. CODE: card C3, `update` in gain form.

items.anchor: introduce a new term
items.note: DERIVE: K = W1 = σ̄²/(σ̄² + σ_z²) = P̄/(P̄ + Q_meas). Read it as "my uncertainty / total uncertainty". The denominator is the innovation variance S, which the chapter never names; NIS uses it.

items.anchor: is the Kalman gain. It's the crux of the Kalman filter
items.note: DEFINE: K, a scalar in [0, 1] here. In n-D it becomes the n×m matrix P̄Hᵀ S⁻¹ (Thrun Table 3.1, gold package). Same job: how far to move along the residual.

items.anchor: If the measurement is nine times more accurate than the prior
items.note: TEST: book example: σ̄² = 9σ_z² gives K = 9/10. A unit test with P̄ = 9, Q_meas = 1 and any z checks the gain form against the Bayes form.

items.anchor: We can also express the variance in terms of the Kalman gain
items.note: DERIVE: σ̄²σ_z²/(σ̄² + σ_z²) = Kσ_z² = (1 − K)σ̄². Derive all three; Kσ_z² is the form that shows P < Q_meas always. CODE: card C3. TEST: all three agree to 1e-12.

items.anchor: We can understand this by looking at this chart
items.note: FIGURE: the residual chart. the red line from x_{t−1} to the prior x̄_t is predict; the vertical segment from x̄_t to z is the residual y; the posterior sits K of the way up. PITFALL (book): the label reads "y = z − −x̄_t", a doubled minus; it is y = z − x̄_t.

items.anchor: K = P / (P + R)  # Kalman gain
items.note: DERIVE: the gain-form update. Labbe's R here is the measurement variance = Q_meas in the package. CODE: card C3, `update(x, P, z, Q_meas)`. PITFALL: in n-D, P = (1 − K)P loses symmetry and definiteness under round-off; the gold package uses Joseph form.

items.anchor: dx, Q = movement # mean and variance of movement
items.note: DEFINE: Labbe's Q = process variance = R_proc in the package. Never write a bare Q in your code; the next book you open (Thrun) uses Q for the measurement.

items.anchor: is nearly universally used for the measurement noise
items.note: PITFALL: "nearly universally" is the book's claim. Thrun (gold package) uses R for process and Q for measurement, the reverse. That collision is why this repo writes R_proc and Q_meas everywhere.

items.anchor: orthogonal projection
items.note: LINK: Kalman's own derivation: the posterior is the linear minimum-variance estimate, the projection of x onto the span of the measurements. Labbe ch. 7 (Kalman Filter Math) for what the book gives; not needed for this package.

items.anchor: Full Description of the Algorithm
items.note: Must read, 10 min. Take the generic init / predict / update recipe and the two tables on p. 153; every filter in Labbe and Thrun is an instance.

items.anchor: Every filter in this book implements the same algorithm, just with different mathematical details
items.note: WHY: g-h, discrete Bayes, KF, EKF, UKF, particle filter: predict with a model, compare to a measurement, move part way. LINK: Thrun Table 2.1 (Bayes filter) is this recipe in its general form.

items.anchor: Compute residual between estimated state and measurement
items.note: DEFINE: residual y = z − x̄ (innovation). ROBOT: when the state is a heading, wrap y with `wrap()` from models.py before it meets K; a 359° vs 1° residual of 358° is the classic bug. Not needed in this chapter (no angles).

items.anchor: Compute scaling factor based on whether the measurement
items.note: WHY: step 3 is the only place the filter differs from a g-h filter: K is computed from variances at each step instead of being picked by you.

items.anchor: ¯x = x + dx
items.note: DERIVE: predict table, Kalman form: x̄ = x + dx, P̄ = P + Q (Labbe's Q = R_proc). CODE: card C1. Compare column by column with the Bayes-form column to the left.

items.anchor: x = ¯x + Ky
items.note: DERIVE: update table, Kalman form: y = z − x̄, K = P̄/(P̄ + R), x = x̄ + Ky, P = (1 − K)P̄, with Labbe's R = Q_meas. These four lines are the scalar Thrun Table 3.1 with A = C = 1. CODE: card C3.

items.anchor: Comparison with g-h and discrete Bayes Filters
items.note: Skim, 5 min. Uniform error bars (g-h) vs Gaussian (KF) vs arbitrary histogram (discrete Bayes): expressiveness against tractability.

items.anchor: Using a uniform or Gaussian distribution is a modeling choice
items.note: WHY: the Gaussian is chosen because sum and product stay closed (p. 135), not because sensors are Gaussian. ROBOT: lidar ranges have a long tail from multipath; that tail is where gating earns its keep.

items.anchor: But with this power comes mathematical intractability
items.note: LINK: the histogram's expressiveness costs you closed forms and analysis. The particle filter (Thrun ch. 4, Labbe ch. 12) buys it back with samples.

items.anchor: Introduction to Designing a Filter
items.note: Must read, 15 min. Take the smug filter (p. 156) and the warning about spec sheets (p. 158).

items.anchor: sensor exhibits white noise with a standard deviation of 0.13 volts
items.note: DEFINE: σ = 0.13 V, so Q_meas = 0.13² = 0.0169 V². The code passes voltage_std**2 (p. 157), correctly squared.

items.anchor: This is called a smug
items.note: PITFALL: zero process variance makes P → 0 and K → 0: the filter stops listening. ROBOT: an IMU gyro bias modelled as constant with R_proc = 0 will be estimated once and never track the temperature drift. Give every state a random walk.

items.anchor: This is the expected variance in the change of voltage
items.note: WHY: R_proc is a per-step variance of how much the true value changes, not sensor noise. Thermocouple in a reaction chamber: large; room air: tiny (the book's examples). ROBOT: the same reasoning sets the gyro-bias random-walk variance.

items.anchor: actual_voltage = 16.3
items.note: PITFALL (book): the code uses 16.3 V; the text on p. 158 compares the result with 16.4. 16.3 is right.

items.anchor: Variance converges to 0.005
items.note: TEST: book output; the map's fixed-point run gives P∞ = 0.00537 V² for R_proc = 0.0025, Q_meas = 0.0169 (σ ≈ 0.073 V, well under the sensor's 0.13 V).

items.anchor: x = update(prior, gaussian(z, voltage_std**2))
items.note: CODE: the likelihood takes a variance. Passing voltage_std instead of voltage_std**2 is the most common bug in a first KF.

items.anchor: which is quite close to the
items.note: PITFALL (book): "16.4 used by the volt() function" should be 16.3 (code on p. 156). The 16.213 is from the author's single run; your run will differ.

items.anchor: Values are often maximums
items.note: WHY: a datasheet σ is a bound or a typical value, not your part. ROBOT: measure Q_meas from a static log (and, for an IMU, an Allan-variance plot) on the robot, with its own mounting and wiring.

items.anchor: modeling the performance of your sensors is one of the harder
items.note: WHY: the filter equations are five lines; the variances are the engineering. Every bad result in p. 159–167 is a wrong variance or a wrong model, never a wrong equation.

items.anchor: Animation
items.note: Skip; a GIF that does not render in the PDF. The session shows the same predict/update breathing of the Gaussian.

items.anchor: varies with time. As the filter becomes more confident in its state
items.note: WHY: K_t starts near 1 and settles to K∞; a g-h filter uses a fixed g from the start. Once K settles the KF is a g-h filter, which is the fixed-gain filter on p. 167.

items.anchor: Example: Extreme Amounts of Noise
items.note: Must read, 5 min. Take: huge Q_meas is harmless when the process model is exactly right.

items.anchor: sensor_var = 300.**2
items.note: DEFINE: Q_meas = 90 000 m², R_proc = 2. The map's fixed-point run gives K∞ = 0.0047: each reading moves the estimate by half a percent of the residual.

items.anchor: We get a nearly straight line because our process error is small
items.note: PITFALL: the line is straight because the simulated dog moves exactly +1 per step, which is also the filter's model. The result proves nothing about a dog that turns or speeds up; the next example shows it.

items.anchor: Example: Incorrect Process Variance
items.note: Must read, 10 min. The most important failure in the chapter: a too-small R_proc diverges and nothing inside the filter says so.

items.anchor: If you lie to the filter by setting this number artificially low
items.note: WHY: R_proc is how much the filter lets the world change. Too small and the gain collapses (map run: K∞ = 0.00705 for R_proc = 0.001, Q_meas = 20) while the dog accelerates.

items.anchor: dog = DogSimulation(pos.mean, 1, sensor_var, process_var*10000)
items.note: PITFALL: two mismatches at once. The simulated dog has process variance 10 (0.001 × 10 000) and gains 0.04 m/step of velocity each step; the filter assumes 0.001 and constant +1. The exercises separate the two.

items.anchor: The filter does not 'notice' that it is diverging from the measurements
items.note: WHY: P comes from the variances alone (p. 138), so the filter's confidence keeps rising while its error grows. TEST: the normalised innovation y²/S (NIS) should average 1; here it grows without bound. The exercises compute it; this chapter does not.

items.anchor: math requires that the variances correctly describe your system
items.note: WHY: the KF is optimal for the model you give it. ROBOT: when a drone altitude filter lags in a fast climb, raise R_proc or add a velocity state before touching anything else.

items.anchor: Example: Bad Initial Estimate
items.note: Must read, 10 min with the next example. Take: a wrong x0 is a transient whose length is set by K∞; initialise from the first measurement.

items.anchor: I'll reduce the sensor variance to 30
items.note: PITFALL (book): the code sets sensor_var = 5.**2 = 25, and the text on p. 162 says σ² = 5². Use 25 when you reproduce the plot.

items.anchor: after only the first step we have changed our position estimate from 1000 m
items.note: WHY: P̄ = 500 + 2 against Q_meas = 25 gives K = 0.953 on step 1 (run in this repo), so the prior keeps 4.7% of its weight: about 47 m of the 1000 m error survives. Hence "roughly 50 m".

items.anchor: In practice we would likely assign the first measurement from the sensor as the initial
items.note: ROBOT: standard practice: x0 = z₀, P0 = Q_meas (the first reading's own variance). Do the same for a GPS fix or a first lidar pose.

items.anchor: still converges so long as the filter variances are chosen to match
items.note: PITFALL: P0 = 500 claims a 22 m σ while the error is 1000 m. It recovers here only because Q_meas is small and K₁ ≈ 1. An overconfident P0 with a noisy sensor is the next example.

items.anchor: Example: Large Noise and Bad Initial Estimate
items.note: Must read (with the previous example). Take how slowly a bad x0 decays when K∞ is small.

items.anchor: By my eye it takes the filter 400 or so
items.note: WHY: after the first steps the error shrinks by a factor (1 − K) per step. With K∞ = 0.00813 (map run, Q_meas = 30 000) the time constant is about 1/K∞ ≈ 123 steps, so hundreds of steps to wash out 1000 m.

items.anchor: pos = gaussian(zs[0], 500.)
items.note: PITFALL: initialising from z₀ is right, but P0 = 500 is then a lie: z₀ has variance 30 000. The book blames the slow runs (200 steps, p. 164) on the noise in the first measurement; our reading is that P0 = 500 is what lets that noise persist. With P0 = Q_meas the filter knows how little it knows.

items.anchor: None have the enormous errors in these examples
items.note: WHY: the examples are deliberately extreme. Real Q_meas values are small; real trouble comes from R_proc and model mismatch (p. 160), not from sensor noise.

items.anchor: Exercise: Interactive Plots
items.note: EXERCISE: this becomes the package session (sliders for x0, Q_meas, velocity, R_proc). Do not write the ipywidgets version.

items.anchor: pos = update(pos, gaussian(z, sensor_noise))

items.anchor: Exercise - Nonlinear Systems
items.note: EXERCISE: in the package, reframed. Read the discussion on p. 167 critically: see the notes on p. 166 and p. 167.

items.anchor: Do you suppose that this filter works well or poorly with nonlinear systems?
items.note: PITFALL: z = 2 sin(i/3) is a time-varying signal measured directly, not a nonlinear system. Model and measurement are both linear in x; the issue is model mismatch. Nonlinearity means f or h is nonlinear in the state (Labbe ch. 9).

items.anchor: process_model = gaussian(1., process_var)
items.note: PITFALL: the model adds +1 to the estimate every step; the signal has no such drift. That injected displacement is what pushes the filter above the sine. The exercise isolates it from the lag that a small R_proc causes.

items.anchor: whereas our process model assumes constant velocity
items.note: PITFALL (book): this filter has no velocity state; its model is x̄ = x + 1. The lag argument is real for a slow gain, but the dominant error here is the wrong +1. map.md open question 2.

items.anchor: Fixed Gain Filters
items.note: Must read, 5 min. Take: constant R_proc and Q_meas → P and K converge → hard-code K∞. Then compute K∞ instead of guessing it.

items.anchor: This will always happen if the variance of the measurement and process is a constant
items.note: DERIVE: the fixed point P² + R_proc·P − R_proc·Q_meas = 0 (map.md), K∞ = (P∞ + R_proc)/(P∞ + R_proc + Q_meas). No simulation needed. CODE: card C4, `steady_state`.

items.anchor: do not underestimate the value of spending one dollar less
items.note: ROBOT: a fixed-gain filter is an α filter (α = K∞): one multiply-add per step, fits fixed-point on a motor-driver MCU. LINK: in n-D the same idea is the steady-state KF, gains from the discrete algebraic Riccati equation.

items.anchor: experimentally derived Kalman gain
items.note: PITFALL (book): K = 0.13232 matches none of the filters in this chapter (map.md steady-state table: 0.5, 0.48, 0.32, 0.0047, 0.007, 0.25, 0.008). Treat it as an arbitrary example; compute your own K∞ from the variances (card C4).

items.anchor: If the variances converge to a single value so does the Kalman gain
items.note: WHY: K is a function of P̄ only, so a constant P̄∞ gives a constant K∞. PITFALL: the fixed-gain filter has no P, so it cannot gate outliers or report its own uncertainty.
